I got the follwing suggestion. Tell me what you think. Feature: safe, ergonomic external UI updates (actor-thread signal handoff)
Context
Pathland 0.2.1, as used by Quarkus 3.39+ and Spring Boot hosts. Views are authored in the Kotlin DSL with WritableSignal, computed, and effect. Pathland signals are documented as single-threaded by contract, and PathlandRegistry serializes all session work on a single actor thread.
Problem
External event sources — Kafka/SmallRye @Incoming consumers, scheduled jobs, DB notifications, websocket clients, etc. — run on non-Pathland threads. There is no supported way to update a live session’s signal from such a thread.
A signal injected into the Pathland environment can physically be set from a consumer thread, but that runs the emitter/binding effects and delta generation on the consumer thread while the session actor may be rendering the same tree. That is a data race. The current public alternatives are all unsatisfactory:
- an explicit UI Refresh button (requires a user click),
- resync(...), which only re-emits the retained tree and does not re-run body(),
- reflection into private registry/session state,
- client-side script hacks.
This is a common server-driven-UI requirement and should be a first-class Pathland feature.
Goal
Add a thread-safe, non-blocking API for external code to update live Pathland UIs while preserving the actor model and producing normal fine-grained deltas.
Proposed design
1. Core actor primitive
Add an explicit actor handoff to the server core:
public interface PathlandSession {
    /** Safe from any thread; runs on this session's actor. */
    void submit(Runnable task);
}

public final class PathlandRegistry {
    Set<String> sessionIds();
    void submitAll(Consumer<PathlandSession> action);
    AutoCloseable onSession(Consumer<PathlandSession> onOpen,
                            Consumer<PathlandSession> onClose);
}
Requirements: work is serialized on the existing actor, dropped after shutdown, and exceptions are logged without killing the session.
2. App-level signal hub
Provide an app-scoped hub with a canonical value and per-session mirrors:
public interface PathlandSignalHub {
    /** Safe from any thread; non-blocking, coalescing. */
    <T> void publish(String name, T value);

    <T> WritableSignal<T> appSignal(String name, T initial);
}
- publish never touches a session’s reactive graph directly.
- It schedules, per subscribed session, an update of that session’s local WritableSignal on the session actor.
- The local signal triggers the existing effect/delta path.
- Latest-wins per (session, signal); bounded queues; metrics for published/coalesced/dropped.
- Subscribe on session open, unsubscribe on close; no work after close.
3. Environment integration
Bind a session-scoped SessionSignals object at the root, similar to Platform.ACTIVE_PATH:
EnvironmentKey<SessionSignals> SESSION_SIGNALS =
        EnvironmentKey.of("pathland.sessionSignals");

public interface SessionSignals {
    <T> Signal<T> signal(String name, T initial);
    void submit(Runnable task);
}
View usage:
val count = Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS)
    .signal("customer-events.count", 0)

Text(computed { "Customer events consumed: ${count.get()}" })
External producer:
@Incoming("customer-channel")
void onCustomer(CustomerCreatedEvent event) {
    hub.publish("customer-events.count", counter.incrementAndGet());
}
The host should bind SessionSignals automatically; app authors should not need per-session plumbing.
4. Multi-node
Design publish to be node-agnostic. A follow-up can back it with Redis pub/sub or a versioned state store, with each node fanning out to its local sessions. Ignore stale/duplicate updates. Pathland already has pathland-state-redis to build on.
Non-goals / constraints
- Do not make WritableSignal.set asynchronous or magically thread-safe; keep its synchronous semantics.
- Do not share one global WritableSignal across sessions without per-effect actor dispatch; that creates cross-session races.
- No breaking changes to existing public APIs; prefer additive APIs.
- Keep both Quarkus and Spring Boot hosts working; the core must stay framework-agnostic.
- No unbounded queues or blocking producers.
Acceptance criteria
- A Kafka/SmallRye consumer can call hub.publish("counter", n) from its worker thread, and a live view’s computed text updates via a small delta — no Refresh button, no resync.
- All signal reads, writes, and effect execution occur on the session actor thread; add an assertion/test for this.
- Multiple sessions receive independent updates; closing a session cancels pending updates.
- Rapid updates coalesce to the latest value without unbounded memory growth.
- Works in both Quarkus and Spring Boot test harnesses; include a Quarkus test with a background thread and a multi-session test.
- Docs: API documentation plus a short “external updates” guide using the Kafka example; update any relevant spec/architecture notes.

- lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/dev/pathland/server/PathlandSession.java

- lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/core/Environment.kt

- lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-starter/
- Existing tests under lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/test/ and lib/java/pathland-quarkus/src/test/
Suggested implementation order
1. Add submit / onSession / sessionIds to the server core with tests.
2. Add PathlandSignalHub, session-local mirrors, and automatic environment binding; add unit and integration tests.
3. Add coalescing metrics and shutdown/close behavior.
4. Add the Kafka example and docs.
5. Discuss Redis-backed fan-out as a follow-up.
First step
Read the current registry/session/emitter/signal/environment implementation, then propose a concrete implementation plan — API names, files, tests, and any spec conflicts — before writing code.

## Yes — `topic` belongs next to `signal` and `computed`

It's the right level of abstraction: one factory, one return type, no new ceremony. It also reads naturally in both places:

```kotlin
// In a view
val name = topic("customer.name", customerId, initialName)

// In the publisher
hub.publish("customer.name", customerId, updatedName)
```

## Proposed shape

Add to the DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`) and the core `Signals` object:

```kotlin
// Global / fully-qualified topic
fun <T> topic(name: String, initial: T): Signal<T>

// Topic scoped to a subject (customer, order, conversation, …)
fun <T> topic(name: String, subject: Any, initial: T): Signal<T>
```

That gives you both styles, and your original snippet still works:

```kotlin
val consumed = topic("events.consumed", 0L)                       // key = "events.consumed"
val name     = topic("customer.name", customerId, initialName)    // key = ("customer.name", customerId)

// Same thing, fully qualified if you prefer composing it yourself:
val name     = topic("customer.$customerId.name", initialName)
```

```java
hub.publish("events.consumed", count);
hub.publish("customer.name", customerId, updatedName);
```

## What it returns

A read-only `Signal<T>`, backed by a session-local mirror:

```kotlin
Text(name)                                   // Text(Signal<String>)
ForEach(orders) { OrderCard(it) }            // ForEach(Signal<List<Order>>)
Text(orders.map { "${it.size} orders" })     // Signal.map
```

`publish` updates the mirror on the session's actor, so existing effects, bindings, and deltas work unchanged. Only sessions that called `topic` with the same key are updated — the lookup is by `(name, subject)`, so it's targeted, not broadcast.

## The tradeoff

This is stringly typed: a typo in `"customer.name"` on one side silently routes nowhere. Mitigations that keep the DX:

- Put topic names in constants next to the domain type:
  ```kotlin
  object CustomerTopics {
      const val NAME = "customer.name"
      const val ORDERS = "customer.orders"
  }
  ```
- `topic<T>` records the payload type on first subscription; a `publish` with the wrong type is rejected and reported via telemetry rather than corrupting the signal.
- Add a `published with zero subscribers` metric (rate-limited debug log in dev) so a mistyped topic is visible.
- If you later want compile-time topic safety, a typed `Topic<T>` wrapper can sit on top without changing the `topic(...)`/`publish(...)` shape.

## Lifecycle and semantics

- Session-scoped; `topic` is idempotent per `(name, subject)`, so calling it in `body()` or as a field is safe.
- `initial` seeds the signal; subsequent changes arrive via `hub.publish`.
- Publishes are coalesced per session (latest-wins) and applied on the actor.
- An `unsubscribe(name, subject)` escape hatch exists; session close drops everything.
- SSR sessions read their local mirror for the first paint but don't register with the hub.

## Implementation delta

- `SessionSubscriptions` + `SessionContext` interfaces in `pathland-view-core` (so `Signals.topic` can resolve the current session without server-core depending on it).
- `Signals.topic` (core static) and top-level `topic` (DSL) delegating to it.
- `PathlandSession` local mirrors, context thread-local around mount/dispatch/drain, hub registration, close cleanup.
- `PathlandSignalHub` registry-scoped; `publish(name, value)` and `publish(name, subject, value)`.
- Starters produce the root-mount hub; `PathlandHost.signalHub(mount)` for multi-app.
- Tests for targeted delivery, coalescing, close cleanup, actor-thread application, Quarkus/Spring background threads; docs/status updates.

Two choices to lock the DX:

1. Do you want **both** overloads (`topic(name, initial)` and `topic(name, subject, initial)`), or only the 2-argument form with the subject embedded in the name?
2. Should `topic` return a read-only `Signal<T>` (my recommendation), or a `WritableSignal<T>` where local `.set()` is allowed? A writable one makes local mutation easy but blurs "this value is driven by the hub."
I need it to be stronly typed similar to with SignalKey. And it must always be scoped also.

/**
 * A strongly typed, always-scoped subscription key.
 *
 * [T] is the published payload type and [S] is the subject (the thing the
 * subscription is about — a customer id, order id, tenant, conversation, …).
 * Both are checked at compile time by [subscribe] and

 * Identity is by [name] (not by instance), so a topic declared once and shared
 * across modules — or across a process boundary — resolves to the same
 * subscription stream. Two topics with the same name must therefore carry the
 * same payload and subject types; declare each topic once in a shared constant
 * object.
 */
class Topic<T, S> @JvmOverloads constructor(val name: String) {

    override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean =
        this === other || (other is Topic<*, *> && other.name == name)

    override fun hashCode(): Int = name.hashCode()

    override fun toString(): String = "Topic($name)"

    companion object {
        /** A topic named [name] with payload type [T] and subject type [S]. */
        @JvmStatic
        fun <T, S> of(name: String): Topic<T, S> = Topic(name)

# External UI updates with topic subscriptions

Pathland signals are single-threaded by contract: reads, writes, and effects run
on the session's actor. Background work (Kafka/SmallRye `@Incoming` consumers,
scheduled jobs, database notifications, other transports) runs on its own
threads, so it must not set a view's signal directly.

Topic subscriptions are the supported bridge. A view subscribes to a
**strongly typed, always-scoped** topic and gets a normal `Signal<T>`; external
code publishes a value for the same `(topic, subject)` pair from any thread, and
only the sessions subscribed to that pair update. The runtime applies the value
on each session's actor, so the existing effect/delta path is unchanged.

## 1. Declare the topic once

A `Topic<T, S>` carries the payload type `T` and the subject type `S`. Topic
identity is its name, so the view and the publisher share the same constant.

```kotlin
object CustomerTopics {
    val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic.of("customer.name")
    val ORDERS: Topic<List<Order>, Long> = Topic.of("customer.orders")
}
```

```java
public final class CustomerTopics {
    public static final Topic<String, Long> NAME = Topic.of("customer.name");
    public static final Topic<List<Order>, Long> ORDERS = Topic.of("customer.orders");

    private CustomerTopics() {}
}
```

## 2. Subscribe in a view

```kotlin
class CustomerOrdersView(
    private val customerId: Long,
    private val initialName: String,
    private val initialOrders: List<Order>,
) : Component() {

    private val name = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName)
    private val orders = topic(CustomerTopics.ORDERS, customerId, initialOrders)

    override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 8) {
        Text(name)                          // Signal<String>
        ForEach(orders) { OrderCard(it) }   // Signal<List<Order>>
    }
}
```

`topic(...)` returns a regular `Signal<T>`, so `Text(signal)`,
`ForEach(signal)`, `signal.map { }`, and `computed { }` all work. Subscribing is
idempotent per `(topic, subject)` within a session; repeated calls return the
same local signal.

Passing the wrong subject or payload type is a compile error: `NAME` requires a
`Long` subject and a `String` value.

## 3. Publish from any thread

The starter produces a `PathlandSignalHub` bean for the root mount (use
`PathlandHost.signalHub(mount)` in a multi-app host). Publishing is
non-blocking.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class CustomerConsumers {

    @Inject PathlandSignalHub hub;

    @Incoming("customer-name-changed")
    void onNameChanged(CustomerNameChanged event) {
        hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, event.customerId(), event.name());
    }
}
```

Only sessions that subscribed to `(customer.name, event.customerId())` are
updated. Two customers, two sessions: publishing customer 42's name never
touches customer 43.

## Semantics

- **Scoped, not broadcast.** The hub looks up subscribers by
  `(topic.name, subject)`. There is no global publish path.
- **Actor-confined.** Published values are applied on the session actor, so all
  signal reads/writes/effects keep the single-threaded contract.
- **Latest wins.** Publishes are coalesced per session: at most one drain task is
  scheduled, and only the newest value per subscription is applied. A hot
  producer cannot flood the actor.
- **`initial` seeds the signal.** A new session renders current data from its own
  source; subsequent changes arrive through `publish`. Late subscribers do not
  receive historical values.
- **Session-scoped lifetime.** Subscriptions end when the session closes.
  `SessionContext.current()?.unsubscribe(topic, subject)` is available for dynamic
  subjects; SSR sessions subscribe for the first paint but do not register with
  the hub.
- **Multi-app isolation.** Each mounted app has its own hub; `/` and `/billing`
  never see each other's topics.

## Notes

- Declare a topic once and share the constant. The topic name is the wire
  identity (a future Redis fan-out can route on it); two topics with the same
  name must carry the same types.
- The subject should be immutable with stable `equals`/`hashCode` — an id, a
  value class, or a record.
- For an app-wide stream, use an explicit singleton subject
  (`object GlobalSubject`) as the `S` type; every subscription is still scoped.
- If you need a lower-level escape hatch, `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` and
  `SessionContext.current()?.submit { }` run work on the session actor.

Implemented on branch `feat/scoped-topics` (uncommitted).

## What landed

**Strongly typed, always-scoped topics**

```kotlin
object Customer {
    val NAME   = Topic<String, Long>("customer.name")
    val ORDERS = Topic<List<Order>, Long>("customer.orders")
}

// view
private val name = topic(Customer.NAME, customerId, initialName)
Text(name)

// publisher (any thread)
hub.publish(Customer.NAME, customerId, updatedName);
```

- `Topic<T, S>` — name identity, compile-time checked payload `T` and subject `S`.
- `topic(key, subject, initial)` — DSL + `Signals.topic`, returns a normal `Signal<T>`; works with `Text`, `ForEach`, `.map`, `computed`.
- `PathlandSignalHub.publish(topic, subject, value)` — routes only to sessions subscribed to that exact pair; registry-scoped so mounted apps stay isolated.
- `SessionSubscriptions` — per-session mirrors, latest-wins coalescing, one scheduled actor drain, close/unsubscribe cleanup.
- `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` — any-thread actor handoff; session context installed around mount/dispatch/drain/theming so field-declared `topic(...)` works.
- Starters produce a `PathlandSignalHub` bean (`host.signalHub()` / `host.signalHub(mount)`).
- Telemetry: `pathland.topics.published` / `.coalesced` / `.dropped`.
- Docs: `docs/external-updates.md`; status files and `AGENTS.md` updated.

## Verification

- `pathland-view-core` — full suite green.
- `pathland-server-core` — full suite green; new `TopicsTest` (8 tests: targeting, multi-session, coalescing, actor thread, close, unsubscribe, field/deferred resolution).
- `pathland-quarkus` — full suite green; new end-to-end `TopicSubscriptionsTest`.
- `pathland-spring-boot-starter` — full suite green; new end-to-end `TopicSubscriptionsTest`.
- Full Maven reactor compiles: `mvn -DskipTests install` in `lib/java`.

Cluster fan-out is intentionally deferred; the hub is node-local and `(topic.name, subject)` is the stable wire key for a future Redis-backed implementation.
Cluster fanout? A form of braodcast?

Not to sessions — to **nodes**. The name is the confusing part.

The feature is targeted end-to-end:

```java
hub.publish(Customer.NAME, customerId, value);
```

Only sessions subscribed to `(customer.name, customerId)` update. That holds whether the subscriber is in this JVM or another one.

"Cluster fan-out" would only be the *transport* step between servers:

```
publisher thread
      │  publish(topic, subject, value)
      ▼
  this node's hub ──► local subscribers for (topic, subject)
      │
      ▼  Redis / broker
  other node's hub ──► its local subscribers for (topic, subject)
      │
      ▼
  still only the matching sessions
```

So it is fan-out in the infrastructure sense (one publish reaches N servers), but it is **not a UI broadcast**. No node updates sessions that did not subscribe to that subject. A customer-43 session never sees customer-42's update, regardless of which node it lives on.

Two ways to implement it, if/when needed:

1. **Global channel, local filter** — every node receives every publish and forwards only to its matching local subscribers. Simplest; traffic scales with the number of nodes × publishes.
2. **Scoped/sharded channels** — channel key is derived from `(topic.name, subject)` (or a hash of it); a node subscribes only while it has at least one local subscriber for that key. More efficient, but requires subscribe/unsubscribe propagation and careful cleanup (e.g. when the last session for a subject closes).

Either way, the app-facing contract stays `publish(topic, subject, value)`; the current local `PathlandSignalHub` can be wrapped or replaced behind that interface without changing views. Given that Pathland sessions are currently node-local and there is no shared session owner, this is a deliberate follow-up, not part of the implementation on `feat/scoped-topics`.

So: the current feature is targeted. "Cluster fan-out" would preserve that targeting across nodes. Do you want to design the cross-node transport now, or keep it deferred and just document it as node-local?
I am thinking if we could make a Topic both scoped or unscoped?

Yes — but the cleanest way is to make "no subject" an **explicit type**, not a missing argument. Otherwise the strong typing/value of the scoped API erodes.

Also, clarify the two different things:

- **Unscoped topic**: one signal per session; every session that *subscribed to that topic* updates. This is intentional and still subscription-targeted — a session that never called `topic(...)` for it is untouched.
- **Publish-to-all-subjects**: a publish that reaches every customer/order scope of a topic. That *is* a broadcast and should stay a separate, explicit operation (or not exist). It is not what an unscoped topic is.

## Recommended shape: one `Topic` class, a global subject

Keep `Topic<T, S>` as-is and add a singleton subject for the unscoped case:

```kotlin
object AppTopics {
    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed")
}

object CustomerTopics {
    val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic("customer.name")
}
```

```kotlin
// subscribe
val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)                    // unscoped
val name   = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName) // scoped

// publish
hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count)
hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, updatedName)
```

The overloads are the safety mechanism:

```kotlin
fun <T> topic(topic: Topic<T, GlobalSubject>, initial: T): Signal<T>
fun <T, S> topic(topic: Topic<T, S>, subject: S, initial: T): Signal<T>

<T>   void publish(Topic<T, GlobalSubject> topic, T value)
<T,S> void publish(Topic<T, S> topic, S subject, T value)
```

- A scoped `Topic<String, Long>` cannot be published unscoped: it does not match the 2-arg overload.
- A global `Topic<Long, GlobalSubject>` cannot be published with a customer id: the 3-arg overload would require `S = GlobalSubject`, and only the singleton exists.
- Internally the hub still keys every subscription by `(name, subject)`; the global subject is just a singleton. No broadcast path and no change to coalescing/lifecycle.

`Topic.global(...)` would be a companion factory; the normal constructor stays for scoped topics.

## Alternatives

**A. `GlobalTopic<T>` / `ScopedTopic<T,S>` as two distinct types.** Clearest names, especially for Java:
```java
static final GlobalTopic<Long> EVENTS = new GlobalTopic<>("events.consumed");
static final ScopedTopic<String, Long> NAME = new ScopedTopic<>("customer.name");
```
But it either renames the existing `Topic` (branch-only, so cheap) or leaves `Topic` and `GlobalTopic` asymmetric.

**B. A shared sealed `Topic<T>` interface with both implementations.** Best if you want a common supertype for lists/registries; more ceremony than this feature needs.

**C. `Topic<T, Unit>` / `NoSubject` sentinel.** Same idea as the recommendation, but `Unit` is Kotlin-specific and ugly from Java. A named `GlobalSubject` is clearer.

## Implementation delta if you take the recommendation

1. Add `GlobalSubject` (singleton object) and `Topic.global<T>(name)` in `pathland-view-core`.
2. Add the 2-arg `Signals.topic` / DSL `topic` overloads.
3. Add the 2-arg `PathlandSignalHub.publish` overload (delegates to the scoped path with `GlobalSubject`).
4. No change to `SessionSubscriptions`, `SubscriptionKey`, coalescing, or lifecycle.
5. Tests: two sessions subscribe globally → both update; a third session that didn't subscribe → untouched; a scoped topic with the same name stays isolated; a scoped topic cannot be published globally (compile fixture).
6. Docs/status: add the global example and explain that "unscoped" means "every subscriber of this topic", not "every live session".

Two decisions before implementing:

1. Do you want the declaration to read `Topic<Long, GlobalSubject>` (one class, my recommendation) or `GlobalTopic<Long>` (two explicit types, nicer Java names)?
2. Is the semantic name `global`, `app`, `unscoped`, or `shared`? That word will be in the API (`Topic.global`, `GlobalSubject`).
1: yes, one 2: global

```kotlin

}

object AppTopics {
```

- **Global means "every session subscribed to this topic"**, not every live session. A session that never called `topic(EVENTS, …)` is untouched.
- Internally a global topic is still a scoped subscription keyed by the singleton `GlobalSubject`:

- `GlobalSubject` is **reserved** as an app subject. It is a singleton object, so no app subject value can accidentally equal it.
- No `publishAllSubjects(topic, …)` operation is added. That would be a true broadcast across all scopes and remains out of scope.

Implemented global topics on `feat/scoped-topics`.

## API

```kotlin
object CustomerTopics {
    val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic("customer.name")                    // scoped
}

object AppTopics {
    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed") // global
}
```

```kotlin
val name   = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName) // scoped
val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)                         // global

hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, updatedName);
hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count);
```

- `GlobalSubject` is the reserved singleton (`"@global"`) used as the global scope.
- Two-argument `topic` / `publish` overloads only accept `Topic<T, GlobalSubject>`, so scoped topics can’t be published globally and global topics can’t be published with a customer id.
- Global means “every session subscribed to this topic”, not every live session; no publish-to-all-subjects path.
- Runtime unchanged: the hub still keys by `(name, subject)`, so coalescing, actor confinement, lifecycle, and cleanup are shared with scoped topics.
- Kotlin alias `GlobalTopic<T> = Topic<T, GlobalSubject>` added for readability.

## Verification

- `TopicsTest`: 10 tests green — scoped targeting, multi-session, coalescing, actor thread, close/unsubscribe, field/deferred resolution, global reaches only subscribed sessions, and global/scoped same-name isolation.
- Quarkus + Spring `TopicSubscriptionsTest`: green — scoped customer 42 updates only 42, global `events` updates both sessions.
- Full server-core suite and full reactor compile (`mvn -DskipTests install`) green.
- Docs/status updated (`docs/external-updates.md`, view-core/server-core/starter status, `AGENTS.md`).

All changes remain uncommitted on `feat/scoped-topics`.
